Sequencer.title: Sequencer
Sequencer.summary: Turns a demand signal into an ordered set of equipment commands.
Sequencer.how: The block takes a demand or capacity input and enables outputs in a defined order as demand rises, releasing them in reverse order as demand falls. Configured thresholds decide where each step engages, and minimum on and off times limit how quickly the pattern can change. The result is an orderly progression through available capacity instead of everything starting together.
Sequencer.controls: Commonly used to sequence multiple pieces of equipment, for example bringing on boilers or compressors one at a time as heating or cooling demand grows.
Sequencer.inputs: A demand or capacity input, usually from a control loop, plus an enable input and any availability signals.
Sequencer.outputs: Several on/off or capacity outputs, one per step of equipment.
tuning: The demand threshold at which each step engages and releases
Minimum on and minimum off times per step
The number of steps available
Interstage delay between changes
Sequencer.watchOut: Thresholds spaced too closely let several steps engage almost together, defeating the point of sequencing and causing large swings in capacity.

Staging.title: Staging
Staging.summary: Adds and removes stages of equipment as demand rises and falls.
Staging.how: The block converts a continuous demand input into a whole number of active stages. Stages are added when demand stays above the add threshold for the configured delay and removed when it stays below the remove threshold. Minimum on and off timers protect the equipment from short cycling, and the difference between the add and remove thresholds provides the deadband that keeps the stage count stable.
Staging.controls: Commonly used for staged heating or cooling, for example engaging electric heat stages or compressor stages in response to a heating or cooling loop output.
Staging.inputs: A demand input from a loop or calculation, an enable input, and any stage availability or lockout inputs.
Staging.outputs: On/off outputs for each stage, and often a numeric count of active stages.
tuning: Stage add and stage remove thresholds
Interstage delay time
Minimum on and minimum off times
Number of stages available
Staging.watchOut: Setting the add and remove thresholds too close together makes stages cycle continuously, which shortens compressor life quickly.

LeadLag.title: Lead lag
LeadLag.summary: Chooses which unit leads and which follows, and rotates duty between them.
LeadLag.how: The block designates one piece of equipment as lead and the others as lag, then starts the lead first and brings on the lag units as demand requires. Rotation can be driven by runtime hours, elapsed calendar time, or a manual selection, so wear is shared between units. If the lead unit is unavailable or fails, the block promotes a lag unit so the system keeps serving the load.
LeadLag.controls: Commonly used on redundant equipment, for example alternating duty between two pumps or two compressors so their run hours stay balanced.
LeadLag.inputs: Availability and status inputs for each unit, a demand or stage input, and a rotation trigger such as runtime or a schedule.
LeadLag.outputs: Command outputs for each unit, plus an indication of which unit is currently lead.
tuning: Rotation interval or runtime difference that triggers a changeover
Whether rotation happens on a schedule or on hours
Which unit is designated lead after a controller restart
How a failed unit is removed from the rotation
LeadLag.watchOut: Rotating while the equipment is running can stop and start units unnecessarily, so rotation is normally held until the system is off or lightly loaded.

RampRate.title: Ramp rate
RampRate.summary: Limits how fast a value is allowed to change, smoothing sudden steps.
RampRate.how: The block follows its input but restricts the rate of change of its output to the configured limit, expressed as an amount of change per unit of time. A step change on the input becomes a smooth ramp on the output, which continues until the output catches up with the input. Separate rising and falling rates can often be configured so that increases are gentler than decreases, or the reverse.
RampRate.controls: Commonly used to protect equipment from abrupt commands, for example ramping a fan speed command so the drive accelerates gradually after a mode change.
RampRate.inputs: One numeric input carrying the target value, plus the configured rate limits.
RampRate.outputs: A single numeric output that moves toward the input no faster than the configured rate.
tuning: Rate of change allowed on rising values
Rate of change allowed on falling values
The time base the rate is expressed in
RampRate.watchOut: A rate that is too slow makes the sequence lag real conditions, and a safety-driven command such as a freeze response may be ramped when it needs to act at once.

BacnetHardwareInput.title: Hardware input
BacnetHardwareInput.summary: Brings a signal from a physical input terminal into the program as a usable value.
BacnetHardwareInput.how: The block represents a physical terminal on the controller and converts what the terminal measures into a value the logic can use. Its configuration selects the input type, such as thermistor, voltage, current, dry contact, or pulse, and defines how the raw signal range maps onto the engineering range presented to the program and to BACnet. Out-of-range or open-circuit conditions are reflected in the point's reliability rather than in the reading itself.
BacnetHardwareInput.controls: Commonly used for every field measurement, for example a duct temperature sensor, a damper feedback signal, or a differential pressure switch.
BacnetHardwareInput.inputs: The physical wiring at the controller terminal, along with the configured input type and range.
BacnetHardwareInput.outputs: A numeric or on/off value representing the measurement in engineering units.
tuning: Signal low and signal high limits describing the raw input range
Minimum and maximum values defining the engineering range
Input type and sensor curve selection
Calibration offset where provided
BacnetHardwareInput.watchOut: A sensor type or range that does not match the installed device gives a reading that looks reasonable but is wrong across the whole span, which misleads every downstream calculation.

BacnetHardwareInputResource.title: Hardware input resource
BacnetHardwareInputResource.summary: Holds the configuration and scaling values for a hardware input point.
BacnetHardwareInputResource.how: The resource stores the settings behind a hardware input block, including input type, raw signal limits, engineering minimum and maximum, and BACnet object properties such as name and units. Editing it changes how the terminal is interpreted without touching the logic wiring. These are the values written to the controller on download, and they are what determines the reading the rest of the program sees.
BacnetHardwareInputResource.controls: Commonly used when commissioning field devices, for example setting the raw range for a zero to ten volt damper feedback and the engineering range it represents.
BacnetHardwareInputResource.inputs: Configuration entered in the tool or adjusted over the network, rather than wired inputs.
BacnetHardwareInputResource.outputs: Supplies the configuration used by its hardware input block and the matching BACnet object.
tuning: Signal low and signal high limits for the raw range
Minimum and maximum engineering values
Input type and units
Object name and BACnet metadata
BacnetHardwareInputResource.watchOut: Values marked controller specific can be replaced on download, so use the reinitialize controller specific values option deliberately rather than by habit.

BacnetHardwareOutput.title: Hardware output
BacnetHardwareOutput.summary: Drives a physical output terminal from a value calculated in the program.
BacnetHardwareOutput.how: The block takes a command from the logic and converts it into the signal present at the controller terminal, whether that is a relay contact, a triac, or an analog voltage or current. Configuration sets the output type and the range mapping, so a zero to one hundred percent command becomes the correct signal for the connected actuator. The output also appears as a BACnet object, which means network writes at a higher priority can take control of it.
BacnetHardwareOutput.controls: Commonly used to command field devices, for example a modulating valve, an outside air damper actuator, or a fan start relay.
BacnetHardwareOutput.inputs: A numeric or on/off command from the logic, along with the configured output type and range.
BacnetHardwareOutput.outputs: The physical signal at the controller terminal, plus the value shown on the network.
tuning: Minimum and maximum output values
Default or fail position used when the program releases the output
Output type and signal range for the connected actuator
Relinquish default and priority handling
BacnetHardwareOutput.watchOut: A network write left at a high priority holds the output regardless of the logic, and the sequence appears broken until the command is released.

BacnetHardwareOutputResource.title: Hardware output resource
BacnetHardwareOutputResource.summary: Holds the configuration, scaling, and default values for a hardware output point.
BacnetHardwareOutputResource.how: The resource stores the settings behind a hardware output block, including output type, range, default value, and BACnet object properties. Changing it alters how a command is translated to the terminal without modifying the logic on the sheet. The stored default and relinquish values determine what the terminal does when no logic or network command is present, which matters for safe behaviour after a restart.
BacnetHardwareOutputResource.controls: Commonly used to set safe failure behaviour, for example defining that a heating valve output goes to a defined position when the program releases control.
BacnetHardwareOutputResource.inputs: Configuration entered in the tool or written over the network, rather than wired inputs.
BacnetHardwareOutputResource.outputs: Supplies the configuration used by its hardware output block and the matching BACnet object.
tuning: Minimum and maximum output values
Default and relinquish default values
Output type and signal range
Object name and BACnet metadata
BacnetHardwareOutputResource.watchOut: A default that drives the device to full output on restart can cause an unwanted response after a power cycle or download, so it needs checking against the mechanical design.

BacnetAnalogValue.title: BACnet analog value
BacnetAnalogValue.summary: Software analog point that holds a numeric value and exposes it on the network.
BacnetAnalogValue.how: The block holds a numeric value that is not tied to a physical terminal, such as a setpoint, a calculated result, or an operator-adjustable number. Because it is a BACnet object, the value can be read and written from the network, and writes can arrive at different priorities. Whether the program or the network wins depends on how the point is used, so a point written by logic every scan will overwrite operator changes.
BacnetAnalogValue.controls: Commonly used for adjustable setpoints and calculated values, for example an occupied cooling setpoint the operator can change from the front end.
BacnetAnalogValue.inputs: Either a value written by logic, a value written from the network, or a stored default with no wired input.
BacnetAnalogValue.outputs: A numeric output carrying the current value for use by the logic, and the same value on the network.
tuning: The default or stored value
Object name, description, and units
COV increment and reporting period
Alarm limits where alarming is enabled
BacnetAnalogValue.watchOut: If the logic writes to the point every scan, an operator adjustment is overwritten immediately and the setpoint appears not to accept changes.

BacnetAnalogValueResource.title: BACnet analog value resource
BacnetAnalogValueResource.summary: Holds the stored configuration and metadata for a BACnet analog value point.
BacnetAnalogValueResource.how: The resource carries the analog value object's default value, units, object name, COV settings, and any alarm parameters. It defines what the point looks like on the network and what it holds after a download or restart. Editing the resource changes the stored configuration rather than the current live value, so a running controller may not show the change until the point is reinitialised.
BacnetAnalogValueResource.controls: Commonly used when setting up operator-visible setpoints, for example defining the name, units, and default for a discharge air setpoint.
BacnetAnalogValueResource.inputs: Configuration entered in the tool or written over the network, rather than wired inputs.
BacnetAnalogValueResource.outputs: Supplies the configuration used by its analog value block and the matching BACnet object.
tuning: Default value stored for the point
Object name, description, and units
COV increment and period
Alarm enable and alarm limits
BacnetAnalogValueResource.watchOut: Points flagged as controller specific may keep their field value through a download unless explicitly reinitialised, which can leave a site running on an old setpoint.

BacnetBinaryValue.title: BACnet binary value
BacnetBinaryValue.summary: Software on/off point that holds a two-state value and exposes it on the network.
BacnetBinaryValue.how: The block holds an on/off state that is not attached to a physical terminal, used for enables, mode flags, and operator switches. As a BACnet object it can be written from the network at a given priority as well as driven by logic. Its active and inactive text make the state readable to an operator, and the stored default determines the state after a restart.
BacnetBinaryValue.controls: Commonly used for operator enables and mode flags, for example a network-writable point that allows or blocks economizer operation.
BacnetBinaryValue.inputs: Either an on/off value written by logic, a network write, or a stored default with no wired input.
BacnetBinaryValue.outputs: An on/off output for the logic to use, and the same state on the network.
tuning: Default or stored state
Active and inactive text shown to operators
Object name and description
Alarm enable and alarm state where used
BacnetBinaryValue.watchOut: Logic that drives the point continuously prevents an operator write from holding, so an enable switch appears to snap back on its own.

BacnetBinaryValueResource.title: BACnet binary value resource
BacnetBinaryValueResource.summary: Holds the stored configuration and metadata for a BACnet binary value point.
BacnetBinaryValueResource.how: The resource carries the binary value object's default state, active and inactive text, object name, and any alarm configuration. It defines how the point presents on the network and what state it holds after download or restart. Changes here affect the stored configuration rather than the live value in a running controller.
BacnetBinaryValueResource.controls: Commonly used when preparing operator-facing switches, for example naming an occupancy override point and setting its default state to off.
BacnetBinaryValueResource.inputs: Configuration entered in the tool or written over the network, rather than wired inputs.
BacnetBinaryValueResource.outputs: Supplies the configuration used by its binary value block and the matching BACnet object.
tuning: Default or stored state
Active and inactive text
Object name and description
Alarm enable and alarm parameters
BacnetBinaryValueResource.watchOut: Active and inactive text that does not match the mechanical reality, such as labelling a closed damper as open, misleads operators during troubleshooting.

BacnetMultiStateValue.title: BACnet multi-state value
BacnetMultiStateValue.summary: Software point that holds one of several named states and exposes it on the network.
BacnetMultiStateValue.how: The block holds a state number, each number corresponding to a named state such as occupied, standby, or unoccupied. Logic and the network can read the state, and it can be written where the design allows. Downstream compare or select blocks decode the number into the branches of the sequence, so the mapping between numbers and names must match the logic exactly.
BacnetMultiStateValue.controls: Commonly used to carry an operating mode, for example holding the unit mode as off, heating, cooling, or ventilation for the rest of the program to act on.
BacnetMultiStateValue.inputs: A state number written by logic or from the network, or a stored default.
BacnetMultiStateValue.outputs: A numeric state output used by mode decoding logic, and the named state on the network.
tuning: Number of states and the text for each
Default state after restart
Object name and description
Which state numbers the logic treats as significant
BacnetMultiStateValue.watchOut: State numbering normally starts at one, so treating the first state as zero shifts every mode by one position and sends the sequence to the wrong branch.

BacnetMultiStateValueResource.title: BACnet multi-state value resource
BacnetMultiStateValueResource.summary: Holds the state list, default, and metadata for a BACnet multi-state value point.
BacnetMultiStateValueResource.how: The resource defines how many states the point has, the text for each state, the default state, and the BACnet object properties. It determines what an operator sees when reading or writing the mode, and what state the point holds after a download or restart. Editing the resource changes configuration rather than the live value in a running controller.
BacnetMultiStateValueResource.controls: Commonly used when defining operating modes, for example listing the unit mode states and choosing which one the controller starts in.
BacnetMultiStateValueResource.inputs: Configuration entered in the tool or written over the network, rather than wired inputs.
BacnetMultiStateValueResource.outputs: Supplies the state list and configuration used by its multi-state value block.
tuning: Number of states and the text for each
Default state after restart
Object name and description
Alarm configuration where used
BacnetMultiStateValueResource.watchOut: Adding or reordering states without updating the decoding logic changes what each number means, and the sequence then selects the wrong mode.

ComSensor.title: Communicating sensor
ComSensor.summary: Brings values from a sensor on the communication bus into the program.
ComSensor.how: The block represents a sensor or room device that communicates with the controller over a bus rather than through a physical input terminal. Its values arrive as registers that are mapped to BACnet objects inside the controller, so a single device can provide temperature, humidity, setpoint adjustment, and occupancy detection at once. Because the data depends on communication, a lost device leaves the mapped values stale or unreliable.
ComSensor.controls: Commonly used for room sensors and wall modules, for example a communicating room unit supplying space temperature, local setpoint adjustment, and occupancy status.
ComSensor.inputs: The bus connection and the configured register-to-object mapping for the device.
ComSensor.outputs: Several values representing the readings and states the device reports.
tuning: Device address on the bus
Register to object mapping for each reported value
Write priority used when writing back to the device
Local setpoint adjustment range where supported
ComSensor.watchOut: A communication loss leaves the last reported values in place, so the sequence may keep controlling from a stale space temperature unless validity is checked.

IncomingTag.title: Incoming tag
IncomingTag.summary: Receives a value published elsewhere in the program without a drawn wire.
IncomingTag.how: The block acts as the receiving end of a named reference. A matching outgoing tag publishes a value under a given name, and every incoming tag with that name presents the same value on its output. This keeps sheets readable when a signal is needed in several places. The link depends entirely on the name matching, so the value follows the name rather than any visible connection.
IncomingTag.controls: Commonly used to reuse a common signal, for example bringing an occupancy state or an outside air temperature into several logic sheets.
IncomingTag.inputs: The named reference itself, resolved from the matching outgoing tag.
IncomingTag.outputs: A single output carrying the referenced value for local use.
tuning: The tag name the block subscribes to
Which outgoing tag publishes that name
IncomingTag.watchOut: If no hub publishes the name, the target reads nothing. In EC-gfxProgram, Go To Source jumps to the hub — the Trace button here does the same thing and keeps following the chain.
IncomingTag.plain: Reads a value published elsewhere by name (officially a Reference Target). It is the receiving end of a reference tag.
steps: The target is configured with a TagName.
Each scan it takes the current value from the hub publishing that name.
That value feeds whatever the target is wired into.
IncomingTag.example: A damper sheet drops in a target for outdoor_temp instead of running a wire back to the sensor on the inputs sheet.

OutgoingTag.title: Outgoing tag
OutgoingTag.summary: Publishes a value under a name so other sheets can reference it.
OutgoingTag.how: The block takes a value from the local logic and publishes it under a tag name. Incoming tags elsewhere in the program with the same name then present that value on their outputs. Only one outgoing tag should publish a given name, since more than one source for the same name makes the resulting value ambiguous and hard to trace.
OutgoingTag.controls: Commonly used to share a calculated result, for example publishing a system heating demand so several sheets can act on the same number.
OutgoingTag.inputs: One input carrying the value to be published.
OutgoingTag.outputs: Publishes the value under the configured tag name rather than on a drawn wire.
tuning: The tag name used for publication
Which value is wired in as the source
OutgoingTag.watchOut: Only one hub should publish a given name. Two hubs on the same tag means the value depends on which one executes last, which is why the connection report flags it.
OutgoingTag.plain: Publishes a value under a name (officially a Reference Hub) so other sheets can use it without drawing a wire across the page.
steps: A block output is wired into the hub.
The hub holds that value under its TagName.
Any Reference Target with the same TagName, anywhere in the project, reads it.
OutgoingTag.example: The heating sequence publishes heat_enable once; the fan sheet, the damper sheet and the alarm sheet each read it without a single cross-page wire.

InternalConstantNumeric.title: Internal numeric constant
InternalConstantNumeric.summary: Fixed number wired into the logic and not exposed as a network point.
InternalConstantNumeric.how: The block supplies a fixed numeric value to whatever it is wired to, and that value does not change while the program runs. It is not a named BACnet object, so an operator cannot see or adjust it from the network. Changing the value requires editing the program in the tool and downloading it. Values of one or zero often act as fixed enables, and small fractions frequently serve as multipliers.
InternalConstantNumeric.controls: Commonly used for hard-coded thresholds and factors, for example a fixed delay time in seconds or a scaling factor inside a calculation.
InternalConstantNumeric.inputs: None; the value comes from the block's own configuration.
InternalConstantNumeric.outputs: A single numeric output holding the configured constant.
tuning: The numeric value itself
Whether the value should instead be an adjustable analog value point
InternalConstantNumeric.watchOut: Because the value is invisible from the network, a site tuning problem hidden in an internal constant can only be found by opening the program.

SetpointConstant.title: Setpoint constant
SetpointConstant.summary: Fixed setpoint value supplied to the logic as a control target.
SetpointConstant.how: The block holds a numeric value intended to act as a control target, such as a temperature, pressure, or percentage setpoint, and presents it on its output. It is meant to be read as a setpoint on the sheet rather than as an arbitrary number, which makes the sequence easier to follow. Whether it is adjustable from the network depends on how it is exposed in the program.
SetpointConstant.controls: Commonly used to define a control target, for example the discharge air temperature setpoint fed into a heating loop.
SetpointConstant.inputs: None; the value comes from the block's own configuration.
SetpointConstant.outputs: A single numeric output carrying the setpoint value.
tuning: The setpoint value and its units
Whether the setpoint needs to be operator adjustable rather than fixed
SetpointConstant.watchOut: A fixed setpoint cannot follow a reset strategy, so a building that needs seasonal adjustment will be tuned by hand unless the value is replaced with a calculated setpoint.

NumericConstant.title: Numeric constant
NumericConstant.summary: Fixed number placed on the sheet and wired to other blocks.
NumericConstant.how: The block outputs a single configured number that stays the same for as long as the program runs. It provides the reference values that compare blocks test against, the factors that math blocks use, and the fixed times that timers count to. Because there is no input, the output never changes unless the program is edited and downloaded.
NumericConstant.controls: Commonly used to supply thresholds and factors, for example the low ambient limit that a compressor lockout comparison tests against.
NumericConstant.inputs: None; the value comes from the block's own configuration.
NumericConstant.outputs: A single numeric output carrying the configured value.
tuning: The numeric value itself
The units the value is assumed to be in by the receiving block
NumericConstant.watchOut: The same number often appears in several places, so changing one copy while leaving the others behind creates inconsistent behaviour across the sequence.

EnumConstant.title: Enumerated constant
EnumConstant.summary: Fixed state or mode value used to compare against or command a state.
EnumConstant.how: The block outputs a fixed value drawn from a defined set of named states, such as an occupancy state or an equipment mode. It is typically wired into a compare block to test whether the current state matches, or into a select or write path to command a particular state. Because the value is one of a list, it stays meaningful only while the list it belongs to is unchanged.
EnumConstant.controls: Commonly used in mode decoding, for example providing the occupied state value that a schedule output is compared against.
EnumConstant.inputs: None; the value comes from the block's own configuration.
EnumConstant.outputs: A single output carrying the selected enumerated value.
tuning: Which named state the block holds
That the state list matches the point or block it is compared with
EnumConstant.watchOut: If the state list on the associated point is reordered or renumbered, this constant still holds its old value and the comparison then matches the wrong mode.

BooleanConstant.title: Boolean constant
BooleanConstant.summary: Fixed on or off value wired into the logic.
BooleanConstant.how: The block supplies a permanent on or off state to whatever it is connected to. It is used to hard-wire a permissive on, to disable an unused branch, or to hold an input at a known state so the rest of the logic behaves predictably. The value never changes while the program runs, so any branch depending on it is effectively fixed.
BooleanConstant.controls: Commonly used to hold a feature on or off, for example forcing an enable on a permissive input where the site has no corresponding field device.
BooleanConstant.inputs: None; the value comes from the block's own configuration.
BooleanConstant.outputs: A single on/off output holding the configured state.
tuning: Whether the value is set to on or off
Whether the branch should instead be driven by a real signal or an operator point
BooleanConstant.watchOut: A constant used to bypass a safety or interlock during commissioning and then left in place removes that protection permanently.

SimpleCompositeBlock.title: Composite module
SimpleCompositeBlock.summary: Container block holding a complete sub-sequence behind named input and output ports.
SimpleCompositeBlock.how: The block wraps a group of logic on its own internal sheet and exposes only named ports on the outside. Values enter through the input ports, the internal logic runs, and results leave through the output ports. Input ports typically have a default or override value that applies when nothing is wired to them, which is what an unwired composite input falls back to. Opening the block shows the internal logic that actually performs the work.
SimpleCompositeBlock.controls: Commonly used to package a reusable sequence, for example a ventilation or economizer module that appears as one block on the main sheet.
SimpleCompositeBlock.inputs: Named input ports such as an enable, a demand, or a sensor value, each with its own default or override value.
SimpleCompositeBlock.outputs: Named output ports carrying the results the internal logic produced.
tuning: Default or override values on the named input ports
Constants and setpoints inside the module
Which external signals are wired to each port
SimpleCompositeBlock.watchOut: Behaviour that cannot be explained from the outside usually comes from a constant or override inside the module, so the internal sheet has to be opened before drawing conclusions.

Alarm.title: Alarm
Alarm.summary: Detects an abnormal condition and reports it to operators and the network.
Alarm.how: The block watches a condition or a value against limits and changes to an alarm state when the condition persists beyond its configured delay. The delay keeps normal transients from producing nuisance alarms. When the condition clears, the block returns to normal, and depending on configuration it may require acknowledgement first. Alarm state and text are presented on the network so a front end can display and log the event.
Alarm.controls: Commonly used to report equipment and sensor problems, for example raising an alarm when a fan is commanded on but no airflow is proven.
Alarm.inputs: The condition or value being monitored, plus any enable input that suppresses alarming while equipment is off.
Alarm.outputs: An alarm state output for the logic, and the alarm notification presented on the network.
tuning: Alarm limits or trigger condition
Alarm delay time before reporting
Alarm enable and suppression conditions
Priority and message text presented to operators
Alarm.watchOut: Alarming without suppressing while the equipment is intentionally off floods the operator with alarms every night, and real faults get lost in the noise.

Latch.title: Latch
Latch.summary: Remembers an on/off state: Set turns it on and it stays on until Reset turns it off.
Latch.how: A set-reset memory. A momentary pulse on Set drives the output On and holds it there with no further input. A pulse on Reset drives it Off and holds. When both inputs are off the output simply holds its last state, which is what makes it useful for latching alarms and push-button control.
Latch.controls: Typically used for latching alarms that must be acknowledged, for push-button lighting control, and for holding equipment on after a momentary start command.
Latch.outputs: A single on/off output that holds its state between commands.
tuning: Persist, which decides whether the state survives a controller reset
Latch.plain: A memory cell. A pulse on Set turns it on and it stays on; a pulse on Reset turns it off and it stays off.
steps: Set On while Reset is Off → output On and hold.
Reset On while Set is Off → output Off and hold.
Both inputs Off → hold whatever the output already was.
Both inputs On → hold as well; neither input wins.

table.caption: Latch truth table (from the help file)

Latch.example: A momentary light switch sets the latch, the lights come on, and a 60 minute Start Delay pulses Reset to turn them back off.
Latch.nullRule: If any input is Null, the output is Null — not zero.
Latch.watchOut: Turn on Persist if the state must survive a controller reset — and note that a new persistent block needs Reset Persistent Value run once after the first download.
